doc.title: Don Menza and Sam Noto interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 28, 1997

title: Was jazz an art form? Spontaneity
summary: Menza and Noto on how they saw jazz, Noto's love of bebop over Harry James, and the vitality of improvisation.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Well it’s interesting because I’ve often wondered when even with guys like yourself, when you were learning jazz, did you think of it as an art form? Did you think of it as high art?

Yes. It was a creative art form. And I don’t remember using those exact —. but there was a mystique about it and any time I got ready to ask a musician who I thought was accomplished at all, maybe not a jazz player, but when I asked him about the jazz players and how do you learn to do that, they didn’t know. He says, “Oh he just makes that up.”

Yeah. Anything he wants. A lot of wrong notes. He plays out of tune and that. And I didn’t hear that, what I felt was the spontaneity, the inventiveness of it and it was always exciting to hear three saxophones playing on the same horn, same mouthpiece, and they all sounded different. It just didn’t sound like twenty violin players sounding the same. And that isn’t quite true either, you know.
With me, I never thought of it as an art form or that, I just heard it and I said well this is what I want to do. And I thought if I got good enough at this, you know, I could possibly

make a living doing it, which was a big mistake you know. Even like the Charlie Parkers couldn’t make a living, who was, to me, one of the best or the best jazz player around ever. But I dug it. I mean there was some vital — something vital about it. It tells the whole story about life and I mean I just fell in love with it. And before that, I used to listen to Harry James as a great player and everything, but when the bebop thing came out, it changed my whole life you know? And I keep telling all these guys, man, I could have been another Harry James.
The timing was a little off then.

I think the thing about what Sam says, we agree on it a thousand percent. I think it was the unpredictability of the jazz players. I mean you could go there and you never knew what was going to happen. And this is what makes for — puts the vitality in the music.

I play in Toronto a lot you know, I have a group up there, and all college kids come to hear us now, and they’re really into it. The more we get into the music, the more they like it. I mean it’s really intriguing — improvisation is intriguing in every aspect of the word in every business. So when something happens like that man, it’s great, you know, the spontaneity of it and a quick, good idea, no matter what you’re doing, no matter what end of the business or spectrum.
